title: Smoking Linked with Increased Loneliness
paragraphs: Many of the health risks of smoking are well known — it can lead to heart attacks, lung disease, cancer and more. And now research has also linked it with increased loneliness and social isolation, challenging the idea that smoking is a social activity.

The research, presented at the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Congress in Barcelona, used data from more than 50,000 people across 15 countries who took part in the Survey of Health and Ageing in Europe.
The participants had an average age of 67, with 22% reporting that they were smokers at the beginning of the research period.

The participants also answered questions on their levels of loneliness, including how often they were alone, or felt isolated, or felt left out. This was done at the beginning of the research period, and again two years later.

The researchers found that smokers were generally lonelier than non-smokers, even when they accounted for other factors that could influence the results, like age and gender. They also found that smokers experienced larger increases in loneliness over two years.
This pattern was quite consistent across the countries included in the study.
The researchers said smoking may increase loneliness because the illnesses associated with it can reduce people's mobility, making it harder for them to take part in social activities.
Another reason could be that, as smoking becomes more restricted in public spaces, and more people keep their homes smoke-free, fewer social environments are attractive or accessible to smokers.
Researcher Keir Philip from Imperial College London said, "Smoking is not social; our research shows it leads to increased social isolation and loneliness."
Des Cox from the ERS noted that loneliness is now seen as a serious global health challenge, and this research shows how smoking is a risk factor for it.
"We need to do all we can to help smokers to quit and to make sure young people do not become addicted to nicotine," he said.
